strengths: The paper addresses a practical NLP question: how much additional annotation makes smaller adapted models competitive with larger prompted models.

Learning curves across three tasks, 100 repetitions for most configurations, and supplementary training-schedule experiments provide substantially more information than a single few-shot comparison. Reporting unsuccessful configurations, including BERT on BoolQ, is useful.
Appendix B provides model checkpoints, prompts, and major hyperparameters; the manuscript also links experimental code and explicitly discloses evaluation restrictions.
weaknesses: Evaluation independence needs clarification. Section 3 pools and randomly repartitions labeled benchmark data, but provides no audit of overlap with FLAN-T5's prior instruction-training data. Original benchmark training examples can consequently enter evaluation sets. The striking 10-label result requires an overlap assessment and careful distinction between additional adaptation labels and prior task supervision.

The label budget excludes model selection. The Limitations section describes choosing prompts using 1,000 training and test samples, without establishing their independence from final evaluation. Appendix B also mentions early stopping without specifying its validation data or criterion. These omissions affect both reproducibility and claims about needing only 10–100 labels.

The BoolQ prompt in Table 1 asks whether the passage contains an answer to the question. BoolQ instead requires answering the question itself with yes or no; a passage supporting a negative answer still contains an answer. This mismatch could distort prompting-versus-tuning comparisons and requires a corrected-prompt evaluation.

The instruction-tuning schedule confounds available data with actual training exposure. Appendix B fixes 150 steps at batch size four, allowing at most 600 example presentations per run. Thus larger nominal datasets are not fully consumed, despite the discussion describing whole-dataset tuning. Figure 4 explores alternative schedules, but the selected regime's flat curves do not establish general insensitivity to additional labels.

The variance-based break-even criterion is insufficiently calibrated. Although Appendix C acknowledges exceptions to 'always better,' nonoverlapping mean±SD bands do not establish a specified probability of superiority. Six ChatGPT repetitions and smaller test subsets also make variability estimates less comparable. Common evaluation examples and uncertainty estimates for paired differences and crossing points would strengthen this central contribution.

Figure 2's undefined 'random baseline' is approximately 70% macro-F1 on SST-2 and 60% on the other tasks. These values are inconsistent with standard label-independent binary guessing in expectation. The baseline and metric implementation need explanation before the below-random interpretations can be accepted.

The evidence supports narrower conclusions than the headline suggests. Table 2 gives SST-2 crossings against large-model ICL at 3,000–5,500 examples and BoolQ crossings up to 6,000, qualifying the emphasized 100–1,000 range. Three English binary tasks also do not isolate task complexity or model size as explanatory factors. The practical contribution is worthwhile, but corrected evaluation and reanalysis are needed before a sound Findings recommendation.
